body:
💔 She was the mate he didn’t want… until she became the one he couldn’t lose.
Chapter 1
BRIELLE
Nobody hears me.
Nobody even knows I am down here.
They only let me out when one of them is around to watch me.
I belong to them.
Their servant. Their target.
And I do not speak. I have not spoken since that day—the day the rogue killed my mother.

"GET UP HERE AND CLEAN, BITCH!" Audra screams.

Her voice cuts through the door at the top of the basement stairs.

I have been sitting on the thin mattress they call my bed, staring at the dark, empty room they locked me in. The basement is where I live. No one else is allowed down here, and I am not allowed upstairs unless they decide I can be.

There is almost nothing with me. A mattress. A bucket. A few pieces of clothing. Two books I have read so many times the pages are soft.

The lock clicks.

The door opens.

They are waiting above me, so I push myself up and climb the stairs slowly.

"MOVE, BITCH!"

A hand fists in my hair from behind. Audra yanks hard and flings me forward. I hit the kitchen floor with a dull thud.

All three of them are here.

Great.

That means this will be worse.

"Well, well, well," Audra says.

My eyes drop to the floor before I can stop them. Looking at her never ends well. She has already put too many scars on me, too many bruises, too many injuries that never healed right.

"Look at me, slave."

I lift my head.

There she is—my stepmother, Audra. My father married her about a year after my mother was killed. Then he left Audra for another woman and left me behind with her.

She punished me for what he did.

Her daughter, Marissa, is seventeen. Her son, Arden, is eighteen, a year older. Arden does not live here anymore, but he comes back sometimes.

"You are cleaning this entire house while we are gone," Audra says, her lip curling. "I want every room spotless. When you finish, you go straight back to your room."

She makes me think of the wicked stepmother from Cinderella, except there is nothing pretend about her.

Marissa flicks her hair over one shoulder. "And wash my clothes too, loser. All of them. They better be done before I get back. I have a hot date tonight."

I nod and start to get to my feet.

Marissa shoves me down again and laughs.

"Did I say you could move?" she asks. Then she looks at Arden. "Brother, need anything done? The slave is available."

I glance at him.

Arden's face is empty. He does not look at me.

"No," he says. "I should stay here anyway. I have an assessment for college to finish. I can keep an eye on her while you two go out and make sure she does what she is told."

"Very good, son," Audra says. "You need to pass that assessment if you want that university."

Then she snaps her attention back to me.

"Get the fuck up and start your chores. Now."

I rise carefully and take the washcloth. At the kitchen counter, I begin wiping, but Audra's voice keeps carrying across the room.

"So, Maisie," she says, "who is this date with?"

Marissa brings boys here all the time. Audra does not know about most of them. Marissa sneaks them in when she thinks no one will notice.

I notice.

But I have no voice, so there is nothing I can do.

"His name is Hayden," Marissa says.

Arden snorts.

"You mean the new guy who hangs around with that weird crowd?"

"They are not weird," Marissa whines. "They are hot. And Hayden likes me."

I turn to the sink and start washing the dishes they left piled there for me. Their words fade into the background because I force them there.

A few minutes later, the front door slams.

Audra and Marissa's heels click away across the ground outside, heading toward the car.

"I will help you, Brielle," Arden says.

I look over my shoulder.

He is leaning against the doorframe now, watching me.

I smile at him.

"I will take care of the clothes, get them in the washer, and do upstairs," he says. "You handle the kitchen and living room, okay?"

I nod.

I am turning back to the dishes when he speaks again.

"We have to get you out of here," he says quietly. "You look thinner than the last time I saw you. And that bruise under your eye is bad."

I only shrug and meet his gaze.

His eyes are full of pity.

I hate that look, even from him.

So I turn away and keep washing.

Out of the three of them, Arden is the only one who is kind to me, and even then only when no one else is around. When he is here, he helps. Sometimes he sneaks food down to the basement for me.

I have lived like this for so long that I do not know how to escape it. I do not even know how to leave.

Arden sighs and goes to do his part.

I return to mine. I scrub the dishes, sweep the kitchen floor, gather the rubbish, and dump it into a bag. Then I fill the bucket so I can mop before carrying the trash outside.

At the front door, I pause for only a second before opening it.

Fresh air touches my face.

I walk down the driveway to the bins at the end and lift the lid. After I drop the bag inside, I close it and look around.

Forest surrounds the house on every side.

This is the only time I am allowed outside. The house sits in the middle of nowhere, on the edge of the village, far from anyone who might hear anything.

"I could have done that," Arden says behind me.

I jump so hard my hand flies to my chest. Then I turn and glare at him.

He smiles a little.

I shake my head and point at the view around us.

His expression softens. "Yeah. It is nice out here."

He turns back toward the house. "Come on. We are almost finished. Once we are done, I will make you something to eat."

I take one last look at the trees because I probably will not see them again for days.

Then I turn to follow him.

A strange feeling slides over my skin.

Someone is watching me.

I stop and glance back toward the forest, searching between the trunks, but I see no one.

After a moment, I shrug it off and go inside.

Arden was right. We are nearly finished. A few more minutes, and the house is spotless. Marissa's clothes have been washed and are tumbling in the dryer.

I empty the mop bucket at the back of the house and come in to find Arden standing with food ready.

He smiles and holds out a small plate. "Have some."

Pasta and meatballs.

My mouth waters before I can hide it.

Arden cleans up what he used, then sits beside me at the counter with the food he has made for himself.

Twenty minutes later, everything is spotless again, and for once my stomach is full from the meal he gave me.

I check the clock, then move quickly to take Marissa's clothes from the dryer. I set up the ironing board and iron every piece.

Most of her clothes are not meant to be ironed, but I do them anyway. When each piece is finished, Arden carries the clothes upstairs and lays them on her bed.

When there is nothing left to clean, I look toward the basement door.

"Take this," Arden says.

He presses two apples into my hands.

I smile and nod.

"And I grabbed an old blanket from my room at college," he adds with a grin. "You can have it."

I stare at him for a moment, then take it.

I am just about to step down into the basement when the front door bursts open.

Audra and Marissa stumble inside loaded with bags and bags of things. There is so much I cannot tell what they bought.

I try to go down.

Then Audra sees the blanket.

"What the hell are you doing with that?" she screams.

The bags hit the floor. She rushes toward me.

Before I can move, she shoves me.

I fall down the basement stairs, hitting step after step until I land in a heap at the bottom. My wrist takes the worst of it. Pain shoots through my arm so sharply that tears spring to my eyes.

"What the hell, Mother?" Arden shouts from above. "I was giving her my old college blanket. It is supposed to be cold tonight, and I do not need it anymore."

I look up.

Audra glares down at me while tears spill from the corners of my eyes.

"I decide whether she gets anything or not," she says.

She turns toward him, but Arden cuts her off.

"If she dies down there from frostbite, you will not have anyone left to clean your fucking house, will you?" he yells.

He throws the blanket down to me.

Audra slams the basement door.

I can still hear her shouting upstairs, but the words blur together. I cannot tell what is happening anymore.

Slowly, I try to stand.

I forget about my wrist until pain tears through it again. I pull it tight against my chest and breathe through it.

The blanket lies near me. When I pick it up, two things tumble to the floor.

The apples.

The ones Arden had tried to give me.

I gather them carefully and stagger to the mattress. I collapse onto it and drag the blanket over my body.

Then I lie there, staring at the ceiling again.

My life has not been good.

Both of my parents have left me, even if one of them died. It still hurts that my father chose to leave me with a woman this cruel.

I am alone.

Except for Arden, when he is here.

Audra blames me because my father left. Marissa does too. They both used him for his money, but when he went, the money went with him. He sends money for me, but I never see any of it. They take every bit.

I am seventeen years old, and I have never been to school. The only education I had as a child came from Arden. He taught me little things—how to read, how to write. He would give me a book, and I would copy the words from the pages onto paper.

I cannot talk. I have tried, but no sound comes out.

My hair is long and black, falling past my backside. My eyes are blue. Scars cover my body from the years of beatings Audra and Marissa have given me.

There is a large scar on my neck too, but that one is from the day my mother died. The rogue attacked while I was there.

I wish for a different life.

I wish someone would come and pull me out of this hell.

Chapter 2
UNKNOWN
I need proof she has not vanished.
I need eyes on that house.
The pack will stand with me. They all understand what happened with my first mate, and they know why this matters.

"Is that her?" Annika breathed, nodding toward the girl carrying a rubbish bag to the bin.

I fixed on the girl and searched for something—anything—that would tell me I had found her. Then the answer hit me.

Her.

She is sickly pale, too thin, and unsteady in a way that makes my wolf claw at my chest.

The only reason I am certain is the shape of her face, the echo of the woman I lost. She looks so much like my first mate that it hurts.

"Yes," I told Annika. "That's her."

Annika's attention moved back to the girl. Brielle glanced around while she headed for the house again, and I thanked the goddess that Arden was inside.

What has that woman done to my little girl?

The front door closed. I let out a breath and turned enough to find Alpha Mason watching me.

His mouth pulled into a sorrowful half smile before his gaze shifted back toward the house.

"She is human, Julian," he said, then faced me again. "Humans are not usually brought into our pack. But she is your daughter, so she will be accepted. She should have been under our protection from the beginning."

"Does Hayden know, Alpha?" I asked.

Mason dipped his chin. "He knows she is inside. I just sent it through the mind link. He will help. He is taking that human out tonight, so there may be an opening for us to get Brielle out."

"And the evil bitch?" Annika asked, anger sharpening every word.

Alpha Mason looked at her with a crooked grin. "Annika, should I be hearing jealousy in that?"

She growled. I swallowed my laugh as I watched my second-chance mate. Finding out I had a daughter should have been pure joy, but Audra had kept Brielle because of money. I have been fighting to get her back, and still I do not know what Audra has done to her. The child in that house is not the girl I left behind.

"Jealous? No," Annika said. "I want that girl safe. Audra and Marissa are cruel, Mason. Claire heard the way those two women spoke to her and treated her. It was awful."

Guilt punched through me. Brutal and sudden. Tears pressed hot behind my eyes.

"Julian, darling, I'm sorry," Annika murmured, laying her hand on my arm.

"Alpha," Beta Liam said, "the women are coming back now."

All of us looked toward the gleaming new car as it rolled in.

They pulled into the drive looking ridiculous.

High heels, tiny skirts barely hiding their backsides, necklines dropped low enough to make their purpose clear. Yes, the day was warm, but dressing like that to come home made no sense to me.

They went inside. Seconds after the door shut, our werewolf hearing caught the raised voices, then the heavy sound of someone going down. A growl tore out of me, but Beta Liam caught me before I could move.

That woman hurt my baby.

Annika stared daggers at the house. "We have to take her out of there," she said, looking between Beta Liam and Alpha Mason.

Both of them nodded. The hatred in their faces was impossible to miss.

Without warning, Arden came out, slamming the door behind him.

He strode down the path.

"Can you hear me?" he whispered, only just loud enough for us.

"Yes," Alpha Mason answered. "Get to the path. We will meet you there."

We turned away from our hiding place and moved toward him.

Arden was furious. If rage could smoke, it would have poured from his ears.

"Julian, Brielle has to leave now," he said. "That bitch hurt her. When she shoved her, I think she may have broken Brielle's wrist."

Every wolf there snarled.

"How is she?" I demanded. "How is my Brielle?"

Arden's expression softened into something sad. "She's okay for now. She still doesn't speak. I don't think she ever will. She hasn't eaten in days, but I made her something. She couldn't finish it, but she did manage a little." He turned to Alpha Mason. "What's our plan?"

"Hayden is collecting Marissa and taking her out," Mason said. His gaze flicked to Beta Liam, who looked ready to empty his stomach. "Your mother is also going out with another wolf. She just doesn't know that detail yet. Once the house is empty, you go in and bring Brielle out."

Arden nodded, then looked at me. "And you, Julian? What will you do?"

I gave him a small smile. "I will be waiting at the packhouse with Annika."

Arden smiled back, though it faded when he glanced toward the house he had just left. "I still can't believe I share blood with them. Both of them are monsters. After what they have done to Brielle, they deserve to be put down." He looked at me again, and this time his smile held gratitude. "Thank you for contacting me. Since you left, I have wanted to help Brielle. And because of this, I found my mate, Talia."

A low chuckle left me. "No need to thank me, my boy. I'm just glad my daughter has had one decent person near her."

Through the bond, Annika must have felt the ache moving through me, because she smiled gently. The shame of leaving Brielle in that place still sat like a stone in my chest.

"She will forgive you, darling," Annika said. "But you have to tell her the whole truth. All of it."

I stared at the house.

Audra had taken over the home that had once belonged to me and my first mate. Then Brielle had come into our lives. She had been perfect. But that senseless fight between Diana and me had ended with Diana taking her own life and nearly taking Brielle's too. I will hate the wolf responsible for that until my last breath.

One tear slipped free and tracked down my cheek. Annika brushed it away with gentle fingers, then looked up at me with a sad smile.

"Come," Alpha Mason said. "We need to go. Hayden is already on his way."

Together, we turned and shifted into our wolves, heading back toward the packhouse, which stood about forty minutes from the place where my daughter has been living. Arden returned to the house so he could tell us when it was safe to take Brielle.

That stupid bitch stole her from me and convinced the court I was not fit to be her father.

I need my daughter back.

I AM COMING FOR YOU, MY BABY GIRL.

*******************************

BRIELLE
The whole house rattled when whoever had left slammed the door.

For twenty minutes, voices crashed through the walls.

Then music blasted, shaking the house in a different way. That meant Marissa was getting ready.

I am still on the bed, staring up at the ceiling.

My wrist hurts so badly that I think it might be broken.

Sleep and darkness keep dragging at me. I drift up, then sink under again. I am so tired.

I pulled the blanket higher, tucking it over my shoulders. It is thin and useless, but it is still something over me. I know it will not stop the cold from getting in.

A few seconds later, sleep took me.

Darkness is the only place I know.

Chapter 3
HAYDEN
I'm dressed and ready for the ridiculous date I have to go on with a human.

Across the room, my Beta watches me with that irritating curve to his mouth. “You clean up well,” he says.

A warning rumble leaves my chest. “Shut it, Reed. I'm only doing this for Julian. His daughter needs us.” My jaw locks around the words. “I hate that I have to waste a night pretending to date this human so they can get the girl out.”

Reed chuckles. “Still, I bet she'd be fun in bed.”

I let out a short, unwilling smirk because he may not be wrong. The girl has a reputation at school. Everyone knows it. Everyone has had her, or so people say.

“You should have gone in my place,” I said.

“Not happening, Hade. I need to help Arden bring her home.” His grin widens. “Besides, she wants you.” Then the grin disappears, replaced by a hard, serious look. “And your sister would separate me from my balls if I went anywhere near that girl.”

I laugh before I can stop myself, though the amusement dies almost immediately.

“How long am I supposed to stay on this date?” I asked, the complaint slipping out like a whine.

Reed laughs again and starts for the door. “Ask the Alpha,” he says, and that is all he gives me before heading off toward his room.

I turn back to the mirror. Black button-down shirt. Dark jeans. Sneakers. My brown hair is pushed back with gel, and I look exactly how I'm supposed to look. Big frame, obvious muscle, hard lines, six-pack. Most of that comes with being a werewolf.

This is probably the kind of effort I should be saving for my mate when I finally find her. Too bad she still hasn't found her way to me.

“Well, for what it's worth, you do look handsome,” a soft voice says behind me, laughter tucked into it.

I smile and glance over my shoulder at my sister, Delaney.

“Enjoy it while you can. What are you doing while I'm stuck on this stupid date?” I asked.

Her smile stays in place. “I'm going with Reed to help him and Arden,” she says. “She may need a woman there.”

I study her. “She's human. I think she'll manage,” I say.

The look in Delaney's eyes shifts so fast it nearly gives me whiplash.

“You don't know anything about that girl,” she says. “So maybe learn the facts before you start judging her.”

Then she turns and walks away.

What the hell was that supposed to mean?

Delaney is Reed's mate, so of course she is going with him. A lot of wolves in our pack have already found their mates. I am still waiting for mine.

With a sigh, I check myself one more time. Fake date or not, I still have to play the part.

I headed out of my room and went straight down the stairs.

Reed and Delaney are waiting below. Reed is still wearing that stupid smirk. Delaney, however, is frowning. Fantastic. What have I done now?

“All set to go get the girl?” Reed asks, smirking.

I growl under my breath. Delaney moves away from me and disappears into the next room.

“What the hell did I do now?” I asked Reed, turning back to him.

His grin drops. “Let's just say Delaney has a soft spot for Brielle,” he says. “Don't judge a book by its cover, dude. That girl has been through hell and back.”

I stare at him. I know almost nothing about this human girl. Julian said she was human like her mother, but he never cared about that. He loved his daughter. Then the woman he married took her and claimed he wasn't fit to be a father.

I shrug because I don't know what else to do, then head for my car.

I got in, started the engine, and pulled away fast, heading for the house to pick up Marissa.

Because of my speed, the drive only takes twenty minutes. I make it in about half the time it should take.

The closer I get to the house, the more restless Archer becomes inside me.

“What the hell is wrong with you?” I say through the mind link.

“Nothing. We shouldn't be going on this stupid date. We should be looking for our mate,” he snaps. He had never liked the plan, though he had understood why the human girl needed to be freed.

“It's one stupid date,” I tell him. “Trust me, we won't be there long.”

He groans but says nothing else.

I pulled up outside the house. It's small, but decent-looking, with an actual driveway.

I park behind their car and climb out.

At the front door, I ring the bell.

A woman opens it, and I recognize her as Marissa's mother. I force on a polite smile. “Hello. I'm Hayden. I'm here to pick up Marissa,” I said.

Her gaze travels over me from top to bottom, and her smile grows.

Did she just check me out? Oh God. I need to leave.

Archer bursts into laughter in my head as he catches what happened. “She's too old. She's like an old woman,” he howls.

I ignore him.

“Come in, Hayden. Marissa won't be much longer,” she says, pulling the door wider.

I stepped inside and followed her into the living room. The place smells recently cleaned, sharp with bleach.

Footsteps pound down the stairs, and Arden appears.

He looks at me without saying a word out loud, but his voice slides through the mind link. “God help you, man.”

I glare at him.

“Arden, this is Hayden, Maisie's date,” the old woman says.

“Nice to meet you,” he says. “Do you want something to drink?”

I look at him and smile. “Yes, please. Could I have a Coke?”

“I'll go see what's taking Marissa so long,” his mother says. She gives me another smile, then turns and heads upstairs, calling Marissa's name.

Arden watches the stairs for a second before looking back at me. “Come to the kitchen and get your drink,” he says.

We turn together and go straight into the kitchen. It is small, with a door set off to the side.

Arden's eyes flick to that door, and I sense it rolling off him—guilt, sadness, both heavy and sour. “She's in there,” he says through the mind link.

I breathe in.

What catches me off guard isn't the room. It's my wolf.

Archer starts thrashing around inside me like a wild thing. The scent is sweet. Soft. Vanilla.

“MATE!” Archer shouts.

My gaze snaps to the door, then back to Arden. I must look strange because he frowns and mouths, “What's wrong?”

I take one step toward the door. The vanilla grows stronger, wrapping around my lungs, and my wolf loses what little control he has left.

“Go to her,” he roars. “Go to our mate now. She's hurting. She's in pain.”

My hand closes around the door handle.

Then a cloud of stale perfume slams into my nose.

I wrinkle my face and pull my hand back just as Marissa appears in the doorway. A growl slips out before I can stop it.

Oh my goodness. She looks like a slut.

Her black dress is so short it barely covers her ass, and she is balanced on high heels. Her long bleached-blonde hair has been curled and left hanging down the side. And the makeup—I don't even want to start on the makeup.

“You look beautiful,” I said, moving toward her.

I press a kiss to her cheek, and she blushes. The perfume is so thick it turns my stomach, forcing me to step away quickly.

“We should probably get going,” she says.

I nod, but my eyes slide back to the side door.

“We need our mate. Now!” Archer roars.

I shove him back and block him. I have to stay with the plan.

I know who is behind that door. I know I have to help them get her out.

I pull myself together fast. “Let's go,” I said.

Marissa looks at me, and for a second her face drains of color. Then she fixes it, smiles, and reaches for my hand.

She drags me straight to the front door.

We are outside before anyone else can say a word.

“Where are we going?” Marissa asks once we get into the car.

“I thought we could get something to eat,” I said through clenched teeth.

“Anywhere after that?” she asks.

I glance at her. There is no chance I am doing this all night.

“No, sorry. I have to help my father with some work,” I said. Technically, it isn't a lie. I will be Alpha of the pack soon enough.

Her expression drops. “Oh. I thought this was going to be a long night,” she says.

I open the window and start the engine.

I don't answer her. Instead, I look in the mirror at the house where my mate is.

I drive slowly because I need to reach my father through the mind link.

“DAD!” I call.

“You left, son,” he says.

“Yes. Please tell me I can just leave her at the restaurant,” I ask.

My father laughs through the link. “That bad, is it?”

“She is drowning in perfume,” I say. “But I need to ask you something.”

“All right.”

“You mentioned finding my mate after this.”

“Yes, son,” he says. “What about it?”

“What if my mate is human?” I asked.

“Then you accept her as your mate,” he says. “Please tell me it isn't her. The slut.”

“No, it isn't her,” I say quickly. “I was only asking. An Alpha needs his Luna to be strong, and humans aren't strong. They're weak.”

“Your mate will strengthen you, son,” he says. “Whoever she is. Whatever she is.”

I keep my eyes on the road ahead.

“I'll see you soon,” I say. “And please contact me in an hour. Say there's an emergency at work or something.”

My father laughs again through the mind link.

“You might end up enjoying yourself, son,” he says, and then he shuts the connection.

“You okay, Hayden?” Marissa asks.

I give her my best practiced smile. “Yes.”

She smiles back before turning toward the window.

I know who my mate is.

I just have to wait until later.

I focus on driving again as we head for the restaurant.

I don't know whether I should tell anyone yet, but I guess we'll see.

Chapter 4
BRIELLE
I have been asleep forever.
Or it feels that way, at least.

My eyes open when an engine tears away from the house.

For a moment, I only stare up at the ceiling.

Then the pain in my wrist comes back, sharp and familiar, pulsing harder than before.

The door swings open without warning. A figure appears at the top of the stairs.

That scent reaches me first.

Her.

“Well, aren’t you comfortable,” Audra spits, coming down toward me, her eyes fixed on mine.

She snatches the blanket off my body and flings it away like it disgusts her. Before I can shift back, her fingers knot in my hair, and she hauls me across the floor toward the corner.

No. No, no.

I know this routine. I know exactly where she is taking me.

The wall waits there, the one she uses when she wants to break me quietly. Shackles hang from the corner wall, placed there for her lessons. She enjoys it because I can’t speak. I can’t scream.

I twist and fight as she drags me, but it does nothing.

I know what is coming.

“Mother, what are you doing down here?” Arden yells from above. His footsteps pound onto the stairs.

“I’m teaching this bitch what she needs to learn,” she snaps.

She shoves me down hard, forcing me onto the floor with my face toward the wall. One of my wrists is yanked up and shoved into the shackle. Metal closes around it, tight enough to bite.

Then she takes the wrist I landed on earlier.

The pain has been getting worse, and when she pulls it, it explodes through me.

She locks that one to the wall too.

Now I am facing the stone, trapped and crying.

I already know what she will use. She likes the belt.

She whipped me last night too.

Fabric tears across my back as she rips my T-shirt open.

“MOTHER, DON’T DO THIS!” Arden shouts.

“Arden, go back upstairs right now, or you’ll be next,” she snarls at him.

He moves closer anyway.

Audra grabs something before he can reach her and strikes him across the head. Then I see the taser in her hand, the one she sometimes uses on me.

She uses it on her own son.

“That should keep him still for a while,” she says.

Then she turns back to me, belt already in her grip.

There is nothing gentle in the first strike. She throws her whole body into it.

I squeeze my eyes shut and let the hurt swallow everything else. I can’t tell which is worse anymore, my wrist or my back.

Again. Again. Again.

After the sixth lash, she pauses.

The doorbell rings.

She glances upward, then down at Arden. Calmly, she threads the belt back around her waist.

She starts toward the stairs, but she stops before leaving. Her hand clamps into my hair again, and she drives my head into the wall.

The world breaks apart.

Darkness takes me completely.

*******************************

ARDEN
My mother’s footsteps rushed back up the stairs.

I forced my eyes open and began to move, snapping through whatever she had used to bind me.

“Beta Liam, you had better be outside,” I snarled through the mind link.

“I just got here,” he answered. “Why? What happened?”

I opened my eyes fully.

Then I looked at Brielle.

Oh my God.

Her back was a mess of torn, bleeding lines. Her wrist was broken, and blood was running from her head.

That woman had tortured her.

“GET THAT BITCH OUT OF HERE. NOW,” I growled through the link.

I cut him off and opened another link. “Alpha, get the pack doctor ready. My mother has tortured Brielle.”

A furious growl blasted back at me. “She did what?” he shouted. “How bad is it?”

I pushed myself up and went to Brielle. She was barely breathing, but she was still holding on.

“BAD, ALPHA. WE HAVE TO MOVE HER NOW,” I said, panic tearing through my voice.

“DELANEY AND REED ARE THERE NOW. BETA LIAM JUST TOOK YOUR MOTHER,” he roared.

I broke the shackles away from Brielle’s wrists just as two sets of feet thundered down the basement stairs.

Delaney stopped short and gasped at the sight of her.

“What did she...” she started.

A growl ripped out of me. “There’s no time, Delaney. We need to get her out. Now.”

The words came through my teeth.

I looked down at my stepsister. She was unconscious, barely clinging to life.

All of us could hear her heartbeat.

Slow. Too slow.

“We need to kill that bitch,” Delaney snarled.

The three of us ran for the stairs, through the house, and straight toward the front door.

Reed slammed it behind us and hit the button to open the van.

I climbed into the back with Brielle in my arms. Delaney got in beside me, while Reed jumped behind the wheel.

“Hold on,” he shouted.

The engine roared, and the van lurched forward.

I looked down at Brielle. Warm blood was running down my leg. Her wrist was broken so badly that bone jutted from the side.

“She must be in so much pain,” Delaney whispered, staring at her with grief and guilt all over her face.

I met Delaney’s eyes and managed a weak smile.

“She’ll be okay,” I said. “She has to be.”

Delaney stripped off her jacket and laid it over Brielle. As she adjusted the collar of Brielle’s torn shirt, the huge scar came into view.

Delaney froze, staring at it.

I couldn’t stop myself from looking either.

Reed was watching through the mirror; I knew it before he spoke.

“Shit. How did that happen?” His eyes flicked between Delaney and me.

I turned to Delaney. She closed her eyes.

She had been there when they found Brielle. Brielle had barely been alive then too.

A tear slid down Delaney’s cheek, carrying sadness and heartbreak for her friend.

“It happened the night her mother was killed,” she said softly. “The wolf sliced her throat. We found her barely holding on. She was five years old.”

I knew the story Julian had told me when I met Talia. Diana, Brielle’s mother, had argued with him that evening because he had wanted them to move into the packhouse. Diana had not believed it was safe for Brielle. She had left running with Brielle at her side.

That had been the last time he saw his first mate.

“I never knew,” Reed said quietly.

Delaney looked at him. “She was my best friend.”

He glanced back at her, then fixed his attention on the road again.

For twenty minutes, the van flew over the roads as Reed pushed it hard. At last, the packhouse came into view. The pack doctor was already outside with a stretcher, three nurses waiting beside him.

Julian and Annika stood nearby, both wearing the same terrified look.

Alpha Mason ran to the van and tore the door open. Shock flashed across his face when he saw the blood covering both the floor and me.

“Give her to me,” he said.

He took her from my arms and rushed her onto the stretcher. The pack doctor immediately started shouting orders at the nurses and the other wolves around him.

Brielle was pale as a sheet.

Delaney and I climbed out of the van. Reed came around to Delaney’s side.

She broke down then, crying completely.

“What the hell happened?” Alpha Mason demanded, looking straight at me.

“My mother waited until Hayden left with Marissa,” I said. “She told me she was going upstairs to look for something. I went into my room, and when I was about to turn around, she locked me in. I broke the door down and ran to the basement stairs. That’s where I found Brielle shackled to the wall.

“My mother had the taser and her belt out. She forced Brielle’s wrist into the shackle. I heard it snap while I was coming down the stairs. Brielle was crying. Then my mother looked at me, hit me with the taser on the highest setting, and knocked me out with a metal pole I never saw coming. I came around when Beta Liam was pounding on the door.”

I forced the whole nightmare out. Around me, growls rose in response to every word.

“And Alpha,” I added, quieter, “this isn’t the first time my mother has done this to her.”

Julian turned on me, anger rolling off him. “What do you mean, not the first time?”

“She has scars all over her back,” I said. “There was a mark on her collarbone too. It looked old, but it has been opened again and again. It looks like a taser mark.”

His expression changed into something deadly.

I knew exactly who he wanted to kill.

My mother.

By then, more people had gathered outside. Wolves had come from every direction, drawn away from whatever they had been doing. They must have smelled the blood.

“Arden,” a soft voice called.

I searched for it and found her.

Talia.

My mate.

She ran straight to me and kissed me, then pulled back almost immediately to look me over. I was covered from the waist down in Brielle’s blood.

All the color drained from Talia’s face.

“Whose...” she tried to ask.

I shook my head before she could finish. “Not mine. Brielle’s.”

Her eyes widened as she looked back. “That’s a lot of blood.”

“I need to be with my daughter,” Julian muttered.

Then he faced me. “Arden, go shower and change. You can come with us after.”

I nodded.

Annika was trying to hold her mate together. Reed and Delaney were already heading inside.

Alpha Mason looked at me and gave one sharp nod. “I’ll let Hayden know. He wanted to come back anyway.”

Talia and I walked into the packhouse and went to our room. She found clean clothes for me while I stepped into the bathroom for a quick shower.

It took forever to wash Brielle’s blood from my skin, but I got it off.

I dressed immediately, and then we both headed back to the pack hospital to wait for news about Brielle.

When we arrived, everyone was still outside.

Annika, Julian, Alpha Mason, Delaney, and Reed stood in a line, waiting for the doctor to come out.

Chapter 5
HAYDEN

Archer and I are wound tight, both of us hating every second of this useless date when we should be beside our mate.

His fury rolls under my skin, sharp with panic, and it feeds mine.

I need to leave. I need to know who she is, what happened to her, why my mind gives me nothing when I reach for memories of her.

A mind link snaps open, dragging me out of my head.

"Son, get home. Now," my father says. His voice is rough, strained with anger.

"What happened? Did they get her out?" I asked, my stomach twisting before he even answered.

"They did, but it is bad. Marissa's mother hurt her badly. Tortured her. She is in the pack hospital now, fighting for her life," he says, a snarl cutting through the link.

Rage burns through me.

That whore's mother tortured my mate.

Across the table, Marissa is still glued to her phone, whispering and giggling with Sabrina like she has been for the last ten minutes. For once, I was grateful for it. Before the call, she had been pawing at me, sliding her hand under the table and grabbing at my crotch where anyone could have seen. No shame. No restraint. Archer had been pushing up hard, close enough to take over, ready to tear her throat open.

"Text me," I told my father through the link. "Say there is an emergency at work."

A message hit my phone seconds later.

Marissa glanced at her own screen, and fear sparked through her scent so fast I almost looked up before she spoke. "Baby, can you take me home? My mom says someone broke into our house," she says, yanking me back from my thoughts.

I stared at her.

She had just lied straight to my face.

"Sure. Let's go," I said. I caught the waiter's attention and paid for the meal.

We left the restaurant, crossed to the car, and I drove directly toward her house.

"What exactly happened?" I asked, keeping my eyes on the road.

"My mother only went out for, like, half an hour with someone, but she had to go back because she forgot her purse. When they got there, the front door was open. She thinks someone stole something," Marissa says.

"Of course," I said, forcing the sarcasm flat.

Marissa turned her face toward the window.

My mind drifted back to my mate, but part of me kept circling the question of what that bitch had told Marissa. Whatever it was, Marissa was terrified.

I opened another link to my father. He needed the update.

"Dad, the bitch texted Marissa and told her to come home because of a break-in. She said something was stolen," I said through the mind link.

"Keep her there a little longer if you can. Beta Liam just reported that she is losing it, especially after she found the basement door standing open," he says.

A small smile tried to surface. I killed it fast.

"We're almost there, Marissa," I said.

A few minutes later, the house came into view. Beta Liam was outside, pretending to search the area, while that insane woman darted around in every direction like she had lost her mind.

I stopped the car, and Marissa bolted out, running straight for her mother.

"Mother—"

"Say goodbye to Hayden," Audra snapped, anger thick in every word. "We have to wait for the police."

I gave Marissa a smile. "I'll see you at school, Marissa," I said, then turned back toward my car.

Beta Liam said his farewells and started walking up the road. He would wait for me once we were far enough from their sight.

I kept moving toward the car, but I listened.

"She's gone. She's gone," the woman hissed. "Arden isn't here either. He must have taken her."

I reached the car and climbed in, still tuned to them.

"Mother, we have to leave now," Marissa said, her voice shaking. "If anyone sees her, they'll send us away."

I smirked.

Then a scent hit me.

Vanilla, faint beneath something darker. Blood.

I looked around and saw it on the ground.

What the hell had they done to my mate?

I got behind the wheel and started the engine. I didn't linger. I pulled away and drove up the road to where Beta Liam was waiting.

He climbed in, and we headed straight for the packhouse.

For a while, neither of us spoke. The silence was heavy, both of us trapped in the same ugly question: what had happened inside that house?

"Did you smell the blood?" he asked suddenly, breaking into my thoughts.

I looked at him and nodded. "It was on the driveway. What the hell happened to her?" I asked.

His expression hardened. "I don't know. But when I reached the house, the blood scent was coming from the basement."

Archer roared inside me. "We should have gone to her sooner," he growled.

I shoved a block between us because his rage was becoming too much to hold.

I pressed harder on the gas, desperate to get back to the pack faster.

Minutes later, we reached the packhouse and ran for the pack hospital.

We burst into the waiting room, where everyone had gathered. I scanned their faces. Fear, anger, helplessness—every person there carried some version of it.

Then I breathed in.

Vanilla.

I followed the scent down the hall to the room it came from. There, on the bed, wrapped in bandages with tubes running from her body, was my mate.

I froze and dropped the block keeping Archer back.

He pushed forward, staring through my eyes, and whimpered. "Mate. I want mate," he said, his pain breaking through me as he looked at her.

I couldn't stay outside that room. I needed to be beside her.

My hand had almost reached the door when Julian stepped in my way. "Hayden, you can't—"

"Mate," I whispered, cutting him off.

Julian stared at me like he hadn't heard right. "What?" he said. "What did you say?"

I looked around before I could stop myself. Everyone stood behind me, silent, watching. Then my gaze returned to the girl in the bed. She seemed familiar, like a memory sitting just out of reach, but I still couldn't place where I had seen her.

I closed my eyes, and one tear slipped free.

When I opened them, I kept my stare on the girl in the bed and did not look at anyone else.

"MATE," I said, loud enough for the whole room to hear.

Everyone gasped.

Chapter 6
HAYDEN

I could not make myself look anywhere except at my mate.

Behind me, shock moved through the room in sharp little breaths.

"You're certain?" Delaney asked.

I glanced over my shoulder at her. She had been crying hard; her skin was blotched, and her eyes were swollen red.

"I would never claim a mate as a lie," I told her. "She is mine."

Delaney's mouth trembled into a small smile. "Then she's really family now. This time, it counts."

I frowned at her. "What are you talking about?"

She tilted her head, watching me as if she was trying to decide whether I was serious.

"Hayden," she said slowly, "please tell me you remember who she is."

I stared at her. "Who?"

A low growl slipped from Delaney.

"You are such a man. That's Brielle. She and I were friends when I was five. We were together all the time. She used to call you her Alpha."

The name landed, but nothing opened in my mind. I only looked at her, blank and useless, while Delaney dug into her pocket and pulled out her wallet. She slipped a photograph free and held it out.

"Look," she said. "An old picture of the three of us."

I took it.

In the photo, I was sitting with a little girl perched on my lap. Thick black hair framed her face, and her blue eyes were so bright they seemed to shine right through the paper. My gaze moved from the picture to the woman lying beyond the glass. Same black hair. Her eyes were closed, so I could not see whether they were blue.

Then I looked harder and saw the mark on her throat.

*FLASHBACK*

"Move faster!" Julian shouted. "I smell blood."

Branches whipped past us as we ran through the forest.

All of us had gone after them. Diana had taken Brielle and run. We had wanted them to stay with the pack, but rogues had been causing trouble, and Diana had believed the pack was no longer safe for either of them.

I stayed beside Julian, pushing myself harder because I needed to find Brielle. While I ran, she was the only thing in my head.

The trees broke into a rough clearing where our borders met the human town. Two bodies lay in the center of the ground.

Everyone stopped at once, trying to understand what we were seeing. My eyes found the smaller body first.

A broken roar tore out beside me. Julian surged forward and lifted one of them into his arms.

Diana.

She was dead.

I moved toward the tiny body lying near her.

NO.

NOT HER.

NOT MY PRINCESS BRIELLE.

I dropped beside her. Her throat had been cut open, deep and ugly. I pressed my hand over the wound, forcing pressure against it, then bent toward her chest and prayed for any sound at all.

Feet shuffled around me. Too much noise. Too many people moving.

"QUIET," I shouted.

The whole clearing froze.

We listened.

There.

THUMP

THUMP

THUMP

She has a heartbeat.

I looked at Julian, hardly able to believe she was still alive.

Through his grief, Julian gave me the smallest smile. "Our princess is okay. Take her to the pack hospital. Get her out of here. She has to heal."

I did not hesitate. I lifted her tiny body into my arms and ran straight back to the pack hospital.

*FLASHBACK ENDS*

I came back to myself with tears burning my eyes.

How had I forgotten my little princess?

"You remember now," Julian said, watching me with a faint, sad smile. "Don't you? I think all of us knew the two of you were mates. But after I fell apart and married that evil woman, everything changed. We kept moving. You built a life."

His words hit harder than I expected. Brielle should have been mine from the beginning. I should have protected her. I should have been her prince.

Instead, I had forgotten her completely.

How the hell had I done that?

"Alpha. Julian."

The pack doctor was coming toward us with a folder in his hands. All of us turned to him at once.

"How is she?" Julian asked, worry roughening his voice.

"Stable, for now," the doctor said. "She needed a blood transfusion. There were numerous cuts across her back, and I had to stitch them closed. She has extensive scarring over her back, arms, and legs. Judging by those marks, she has been abused and tortured for years. Her wrist was badly broken, so we set it and put it in a cast."

Sympathy rolled off him as he spoke.

Delaney looked through the window. "Why isn't she awake?"

The doctor followed her gaze to my mate behind the door. "We placed her in an induced coma for the moment. She is in too much pain right now. We'll keep her under for a few days and monitor how she heals." His expression tightened. "I am worried about the head injury she received tonight. It may cause complications, but we will not know until she wakes."

We nodded, silent, all of us staring at him.

"Only one person should stay with her at a time," he added. "The rest of you should rest. I will update you in the morning. I will be here all night, and she will have the best care I can give her."

"I'll stay," I said.

The words came out fast enough to startle a few people.

Julian looked at me, but I spoke before he could.

"She's my mate. I need to be near her. My wolf needs it too."

After a moment, Julian nodded. "I'll go, but I'll come back later this evening."

He started to turn away with the others, then stopped and pressed a notebook into my hand.

"She can't speak," he said quietly. "Not since the rogue attack that cut her throat. She hasn't said a word since then."

I accepted the notebook and nodded.

Everyone left. I faced the door, then walked through it to be with my mate. Her scent struck me the moment I entered, powerful enough to make my chest ache, but it settled Archer instantly.

I went to the chair beside the bed and sat down.

Brielle lay before me.

For a long time, I only watched her breathe.

"How could you forget who your mate was?" Archer asked suddenly.

That was the question, wasn't it? How could I?

"I don't know," I said. Memories began surfacing in slow, scattered pieces. "But I remember her now. She was always around the house. Always talking. Always following me everywhere."

"You're an idiot," he said.

I gave a short snort. "Why would you call me that?"

"Because you are. Hopefully she remembers you. If she doesn't, I'm going to laugh my ass off."

The thought stung more than I wanted to admit. Still, I wanted her to remember me.

I looked at her again.

I was sitting on the side of the bed near her cast. My eyes moved to her arm. Scars climbed toward her elbow. One was deep and thick. Others looked like cigarette burns.

Anger flooded me so fast I could barely breathe. I took her hand in mine and stared at the damage carved into her skin.

"How could anyone be this cruel?" I asked Archer.

He was already growling. Then, as he looked at the scars through me, he howled.

He howls for his mate.

I brushed my fingers over some of the marks. The mate bond sparked between us, soft tingles moving through my hand. Brielle did not stir. She looked peaceful, as if pain had finally let her rest.

I hope she wakes soon.

I hope she remembers me.

I want her.

I want my mate.

When I was six years old, I saw a book about the primeval forest called *True Stories*, which contained a wonderful illustration. It depicted a python devouring a wild beast. This is what it looks like when drawn exactly as it was. The book described it like this: "These pythons swallow their prey whole without chewing, and then they can't move anymore. They sleep for six months to digest what they've swallowed." At that time, I thought a lot about the dangers of the jungle, so I drew my first picture with colored pencils. My first picture looked like this. I showed my masterpiece to the adults and asked them if they were scared.

They replied, "What's so scary about a hat?"

I hadn't drawn a hat; I had drawn a python digesting an elephant. So I drew the inside of the python's belly so the adults could understand. These adults always needed explanations. Here's my second picture. The adults advised me to put aside these dissected or complete python drawings and focus more on geography, history, arithmetic, and grammar. And so, at the age of six, I had to give up my promising career as an artist. My first and second drawings were unsuccessful, which discouraged me. Adults themselves never seem to understand anything, and children have to explain things to them over and over again—it's incredibly annoying.

Later, I had to choose a different career and learned to fly airplanes. I've flown almost all over the world. Indeed, geography has been a huge help. I can distinguish China from Arizona in the US at a glance. Geography is invaluable if you get lost at night.

Thus, in my life, I've had frequent contact with many respectable people. I lived in adult circles for a long time, observing them carefully, but this didn't change my opinion of them much.

Whenever I met a somewhat clear-headed adult, I would take out the first drawing I had kept and test it on him. I wanted to know if he could really understand it. But he always answered, "It's a hat." So I stopped talking to him about pythons, primeval forests, and stars, and instead talked about things he could understand. I talked to him about bridge, golf, politics, and ties. This pleased the adult, for he had made a reasonable friend. I lived a solitary life, never truly confiding in anyone, until the accident in the Sahara Desert six years ago, which brought an end to that existence. Something in my plane's engine broke down. With neither a mechanic nor passengers around, I attempted the difficult repair myself. For me, it was a matter of life and death; I only had enough water for eight days.
The first night, I slept in that desolate desert, a world away from human habitation. I felt more alone and helpless than a shipwrecked person in a small boat on a vast ocean. And at dawn the next day, when a strange little voice woke me, you can imagine how surprised I was. The little voice said:

"Excuse me… could you draw me a sheep?"

"Yes!"

"Draw me a sheep…"

As if struck by lightning, I jumped up. I rubbed my eyes hard and looked closely. I saw a very unusual little fellow staring at me intently. This was later the best portrait I painted of him. Of course, the portrait didn't quite capture his radiance. It wasn't my fault. When I was six, those adults ruined my chances of becoming a painter. I hadn't studied painting since then, except for drawing complete and dissected pythons. I stared in astonishment at this unexpected visitor. Don't forget, I was in a desolate desert, a world away from human habitation. To me, this little fellow didn't seem lost. He showed no signs of exhaustion, thirst, or fear. In short, he didn't look like a child lost in the vast, uninhabited desert. It took me a long time to speak. I asked him, "What...what are you doing here?" He solemnly repeated in a low voice, "Please...draw me a sheep..." When something mysterious captivates you, how can you dare disobey? Even though I was in the desert thousands of miles away and facing the danger of death, my actions seemed absurd and unbelievable. I still took out a piece of paper and a pen from my pocket. Only then did I remember that I had mainly studied geography, history, arithmetic, and grammar, so I said to the little guy with some impatience, "I can't draw." He replied, "It's alright, just draw me a sheep." Because I had never drawn a sheep before, I chose one of the two pictures I could draw—the one of the pythons swallowing an elephant whole—and redraw it for him. But the little guy's answer surprised me greatly:

"No! No! I don't want a python; it has an elephant inside. Pythons are too dangerous, and elephants take up too much space. My place is too small; I need a sheep. Draw me one."

So I drew him one. He looked at it intently, then said:

"I don't want it; this sheep is very sick. Draw me another one."

I drew another one. My friend smiled innocently and politely refused:

"Look, what you drew is clearly not a lamb; it's a ram, and it even has horns..."

So I drew another one. Like the previous ones, he refused it again:

"This one is too old. I want a lamb that can live a very, very long time."

I was impatient because I was in a hurry to disassemble my airplane engine. So I hastily drew this picture. I said to him,

"This is a box, and the little sheep you wanted is inside."

To my astonishment, I saw a gleam of joy on my little judge's face. He said,

"This is exactly what I wanted... Do you think this sheep needs to eat a lot of grass?"

"Why do you ask?"

"Because my place is very small..."

"Small, but enough to feed it. I drew you a very small sheep."

He looked down at the drawing and said,

"Not so small... Look! It's sleeping..." And that's how I met the Little Prince.It took me a long time to figure out where he came from. The Little Prince asked me many questions, but he seemed not to hear me at all. Some of his unintentional remarks gradually revealed his origins to me. For example, when he first saw my airplane (I won't draw it, as it's too complicated for me), he asked me:

"What is this thing?"

"It's not a 'thing.' It can fly. It's an airplane. It's my airplane."

I proudly told him I could fly. He exclaimed in surprise:

"What? Did you fall from the sky?"

"Yes," I replied humbly.

"Oh? That's funny."

At this, the Little Prince let out a clear laugh. This made me very unhappy. I demand that others take my misfortune seriously. Then he said,

“So, you're from the sky too! Which planet are you from?”

Instantly, I vaguely grasped a clue to his origins; so I suddenly asked,

“Are you from another planet?”

But he didn't answer. He looked at my plane, nodded slightly, and continued,

“Of course, riding in this thing, you couldn't possibly have come from far away…”

He then fell into deep thought for a long time. Then, he took out the little sheep I had drawn from his pocket and stared intently at his treasure.

You can imagine how intrigued these vague remarks about “other planets” were. Therefore, I tried my best to know more about its mysteries.

“Where did you come from, my little fellow? Where is your home? Where are you taking my little lamb?” He pondered for a moment, then answered me:

“Luckily, I have the box you gave me; it can be a house for the lamb at night.”

“Of course. If you are good, I will draw you a rope so you can tie it up during the day. And a stake.”

My suggestion seemed to offend the little prince a bit.

“Tie it up, what a strange idea.”

“If you don’t tie it up, it will run around everywhere, and it will get lost.”

My friend laughed again:

“Where do you want it to run off to?”

“Anywhere. It just keeps running forward…”

At this point, the little prince said solemnly:

“It doesn’t matter, my place is very, very small.”

Then, with a touch of sadness, he added:

“If it keeps running forward, it won’t go very far…” I also learned another important thing: the planet where he lived was not much bigger than a house. This didn't surprise me too much. I knew that besides the major planets like Earth, Jupiter, Mars, and Venus, there were hundreds of other celestial bodies, some so small they were difficult to see even with a telescope. When an astronomer discovered one of these stars, he assigned it a number, such as "Asteroid 325."

I have important evidence that the Little Prince's home planet was asteroid B612. This asteroid was only seen once, in 1909, by a Turkish astronomer using a telescope. At that time, he presented important arguments for his discovery at an international congress of astronomers. However, because of his clothing, no one believed him. That's how adults are. Fortunately, a Turkish dictator, to protect the reputation of asteroid B612, forced his people to wear European-style clothing or face execution. In 1920, the astronomer, dressed in very fine attire, presented his arguments again. This time, everyone agreed with him. When you tell them about a new friend, they never ask you any substantial questions. They never say, "What does he sound like? What games does he like? Does he collect butterfly specimens?" Instead, they ask, "How old is he? How many brothers does he have? How much does he weigh? How much does his father earn?" They think that's how they know their friend. If you tell them, "I saw a beautiful house made of rose-colored bricks, with geraniums in the windows and pigeons on the roof..." they can't imagine how nice that house could be. You have to tell them, "I saw a house worth 100,000 francs." Then they'll exclaim, "What a beautiful house!"

If you tell them, "The proof that the Little Prince exists is that he's very handsome, he smiles, and he wants a sheep. He wants a lamb, and that proves his existence," they'll just shrug and treat you like a child! But if you tell them, "The Little Prince came from asteroid B612," they'll believe you completely, and they won't bombard you with a bunch of questions. That's just how they are. Children should be kinder to adults and not complain about them.

Of course, for those of us who understand life, we don't care about those numbers! I really wish I could start this story like a myth, I really wish I could say it like this:

"Once upon a time, there was a little prince who lived on a planet almost the size of himself. He wished he had a friend..." To those who understand life, this sounds so real.

I don't like people reading my book so casually. It was very sad for me to tell these stories. My friend and his lamb have been gone for six years. The reason I'm trying so hard to describe him here is so that I won't forget him. Forgetting a friend is so sad. Not everyone has had a friend. Besides, I might become like those adults, only interested in numbers. That's why I bought a box of paints and some pencils. At my age, and having only drawn pythons with closed bellies and open bellies when I was six, I've never tried anything else. Now, drawing again is really difficult! Of course, I want to make these drawings as realistic as possible, but I'm not confident myself. One drawing is okay, another isn't. Also, the sizes are a bit inaccurate. In one place, the Little Prince is too big, and in another, too small. I'm also unsure about the color of his clothes. So I just experimented, trying this and that, making adjustments until it was roughly right. I might have made mistakes in some important details. Please forgive me for that. Because my friend never explains himself. He thinks I'm like him. But, unfortunately, I can't see the lamb through the box. I guess I'm a bit like adults. I must be getting old.Every day I learned something new about the Little Prince's planet, his departure, and his travels. These were all gleaned gradually from various reactions. And so, on the third day, I learned about the tragedy of the baobab tree.

This time, it was about the sheep again. Suddenly, the Little Prince asked me, seemingly very worried:

"Is it true that sheep eat shrubs?"

"Yes, it is."

"Ah, I'm so happy."

I didn't understand why the sheep eating shrubs was so important. But the Little Prince then said:

"So, they also eat baobab trees?"

I told the Little Prince that baobab trees aren't shrubs, but trees as big as churches; even if you brought back a herd of elephants, you couldn't eat a single baobab tree.

The idea of ​​a herd of elephants made the Little Prince laugh:

“Then you’d have to stack all those elephants on top of each other,” he said knowledgeably.

“Baobab trees start out small before they grow up.”

“That’s true. But why do you want your sheep to eat the little baobab trees?”

He answered me, “Well, that goes without saying!” as if it were self-evident. But I myself had to exert a great deal of effort to understand this.

It turns out that on the Little Prince’s planet, like on all other planets, there is good grass and bad grass; therefore, there are also seeds of good grass and seeds of poisonous grass, but the seeds are invisible. They sleep in the soil until one of them suddenly wants to wake up… and then it stretches out and begins to shyly grow a beautiful and lovely little seedling towards the sun. If it is a radish or rose seedling, let it grow freely. If it is a bad seedling, once it is identified, it should be pulled out immediately. Because on the Little Prince's planet, there are some very terrible seeds… these are baobab seeds. They are so numerous in the soil there that they are a plague. And if you pull up a baobab seedling too late, you can never get rid of it. It will take over the whole planet. Its roots can drill through the planet, and if the planet is small and there are many baobab trees, it will shatter the whole planet. "It's a matter of discipline," the Little Prince later explained to me. "When you've finished washing up in the morning, you must carefully wash up the planet, and you must make a rule to pull up the baobab seedlings on time. When these seedlings are small, they look almost like rose seedlings, and once you can distinguish them, you must pull them up. It's a very tedious job, but it's easy." One day, he encouraged me to draw a beautiful picture so that the children in my hometown would have a deep impression of this. He also told me, “This will be very useful if they travel someday. Sometimes, it’s not a problem for people to put off their work, but when it comes to things like uprooting baobab seedlings, it can cause a disaster. I once met a planet where a lazy fellow lived, and he let three seedlings go…”

So, based on the Little Prince’s description, I drew this planet. I’ve never been one to speak in a moralistic tone, but the danger of baobab trees is not widely understood, and it’s extremely dangerous for those lost on asteroids. Therefore, this time, I boldly broke my usual habit of not lecturing. I said, “Children, beware of those baobab trees!” To warn my friends of this danger—a danger they, like myself, have long encountered without realizing its severity—I put a lot of effort into drawing this picture. The lesson I’m presenting is very significant, and the effort was well worth it. You might ask, why aren’t the other drawings in this book as magnificent as this one? The answer was simple: I had tried to paint other pictures better, but without success. But when I painted the baobab tree, a sense of urgency motivated me.

VI. Ah! Little Prince, that's how I gradually came to understand your melancholy life. For a long time, your only pleasure was watching the gentle sunset. This new detail I learned on the morning of the fourth day. You said to me then:

“I love watching the sunset. Let's go watch a sunset!”

“But we have to wait…”

“Wait for what?”

“For the sun to go down.”

At first, you seemed very surprised, then you laughed at your own confusion. You said to me:

“I always thought I was in my hometown!”

Indeed, everyone knows that in America it's noon, and in France it's sunset; you can see the sunset if you get to France within a minute. Unfortunately, France is so far away. But on your little asteroid, you only need to move your chair a few steps. That way, you can see the sunset whenever you want…

title: Your kid becomes the character they love
body: Can't find a screen-free activity your kids actually want to do? Upload their photo, pick a character — princess, knight, fairy — and we turn it into a numbered canvas they paint themselves. Every brushstroke is theirs.

But the little guy's answer surprised me greatly:

"No! No! I don't want a python; it has an elephant inside. Pythons are too dangerous, and elephants take up too much space. My place is too small; I need a sheep. Draw me one."

So I drew him one. He looked at it intently, then said:

"I don't want it; this sheep is very sick. Draw me another one."

I drew another one. My friend smiled innocently and politely refused:

"Look, what you drew is clearly not a lamb; it's a ram, and it even has horns..."

So I drew another one. Like the previous ones, he refused it again:

"This one is too old. I want a lamb that can live a very, very long time."

I was impatient because I was in a hurry to disassemble my airplane engine. So I hastily drew this picture. I said to him,

"This is a box, and the little sheep you wanted is inside."

To my astonishment, I saw a gleam of joy on my little judge's face. He said,

"This is exactly what I wanted... Do you think this sheep needs to eat a lot of grass?"

"Why do you ask?"

"Because my place is very small..."

"Small, but enough to feed it. I drew you a very small sheep."

He looked down at the drawing and said,

"Not so small... Look! It's sleeping..." And that's how I met the Little Prince.It took me a long time to figure out where he came from. For example, when he first saw my airplane (I won't draw it, as it's too complicated for me), he asked me:

"What is this thing?"

"It's not a 'thing.' It can fly. It's an airplane. It's my airplane."

I proudly told him I could fly. He exclaimed in surprise:

"What? Did you fall from the sky?"

"Yes," I replied humbly.

"Oh? That's funny."

At this, the Little Prince let out a clear laugh. This made me very unhappy. I demand that others take my misfortune seriously. Then he said,

“So, you're from the sky too! Which planet are you from?”

Instantly, I vaguely grasped a clue to his origins; so I suddenly asked,

“Are you from another planet?”

But he didn't answer. He looked at my plane, nodded slightly, and continued,

“Of course, riding in this thing, you couldn't possibly have come from far away…”

He then fell into deep thought for a long time. Then, he took out the little sheep I had drawn from his pocket and stared intently at his treasure.

You can imagine how intrigued these vague remarks about “other planets” were. Therefore, I tried my best to know more about its mysteries.

“Where did you come from, my little fellow? Where is your home? Where are you taking my little lamb?” He pondered for a moment, then answered me:

“Luckily, I have the box you gave me; it can be a house for the lamb at night.”

“Of course. If you are good, I will draw you a rope so you can tie it up during the day. And a stake.”

My suggestion seemed to offend the little prince a bit.

“Tie it up, what a strange idea.”

“If you don’t tie it up, it will run around everywhere, and it will get lost.”

My friend laughed again:

“Where do you want it to run off to?”

“Anywhere. It just keeps running forward…”

At this point, the little prince said solemnly:

“It doesn’t matter, my place is very, very small.”

Then, with a touch of sadness, he added:

“If it keeps running forward, it won’t go very far…” I also learned another important thing: the planet where he lived was not much bigger than a house. This didn't surprise me too much. I knew that besides the major planets like Earth, Jupiter, Mars, and Venus, there were hundreds of other celestial bodies, some so small they were difficult to see even with a telescope. When an astronomer discovered one of these stars, he assigned it a number, such as "Asteroid 325."

I have important evidence that the Little Prince's home planet was asteroid B612. This asteroid was only seen once, in 1909, by a Turkish astronomer using a telescope. At that time, he presented important arguments for his discovery at an international congress of astronomers. However, because of his clothing, no one believed him. That's how adults are. Fortunately, a Turkish dictator, to protect the reputation of asteroid B612, forced his people to wear European-style clothing or face execution. In 1920, the astronomer, dressed in very fine attire, presented his arguments again. This time, everyone agreed with him. I'm telling you these details about asteroid B612 and its number because of these adults. These adults love numbers. When you tell them about a new friend, they never ask you any substantial questions. They never say, "What does he sound like? What games does he like? Does he collect butterfly specimens?" Instead, they ask, "How old is he? How many brothers does he have? How much does he weigh? How much does his father earn?" They think that's how they know their friend. If you tell them, "I saw a beautiful house made of rose-colored bricks, with geraniums in the windows and pigeons on the roof..." they can't imagine how nice that house could be. You have to tell them, "I saw a house worth 100,000 francs." Then they'll exclaim, "What a beautiful house!"

If you tell them, "The proof that the Little Prince exists is that he's very handsome, he smiles, and he wants a sheep. But if you tell them, "The Little Prince came from asteroid B612," they'll believe you completely, and they won't bombard you with a bunch of questions. That's just how they are. Children should be kinder to adults and not complain about them.

"Once upon a time, there was a little prince who lived on a planet almost the size of himself. He wished he had a friend..." To those who understand life, this sounds so real.

The reason I'm trying so hard to describe him here is so that I won't forget him. Forgetting a friend is so sad. Not everyone has had a friend. Besides, I might become like those adults, only interested in numbers. That's why I bought a box of paints and some pencils. At my age, and having only drawn pythons with closed bellies and open bellies when I was six, I've never tried anything else. Now, drawing again is really difficult! Of course, I want to make these drawings as realistic as possible, but I'm not confident myself. One drawing is okay, another isn't. Also, the sizes are a bit inaccurate. In one place, the Little Prince is too big, and in another, too small. I'm also unsure about the color of his clothes. So I just experimented, trying this and that, making adjustments until it was roughly right. I might have made mistakes in some important details. Please forgive me for that. Because my friend never explains himself. He thinks I'm like him. But, unfortunately, I can't see the lamb through the box. I guess I'm a bit like adults. I must be getting old.Every day I learned something new about the Little Prince's planet, his departure, and his travels. These were all gleaned gradually from various reactions. And so, on the third day, I learned about the tragedy of the baobab tree.

"Is it true that sheep eat shrubs?"

"Yes, it is."

"Ah, I'm so happy."

I didn't understand why the sheep eating shrubs was so important. But the Little Prince then said:

"So, they also eat baobab trees?"

The idea of ​​a herd of elephants made the Little Prince laugh:

“Then you’d have to stack all those elephants on top of each other,” he said knowledgeably.

“That’s true. But why do you want your sheep to eat the little baobab trees?”

He answered me, “Well, that goes without saying!” as if it were self-evident. But I myself had to exert a great deal of effort to understand this.

If it is a radish or rose seedling, let it grow freely. If it is a bad seedling, once it is identified, it should be pulled out immediately. Because on the Little Prince's planet, there are some very terrible seeds… these are baobab seeds. They are so numerous in the soil there that they are a plague. And if you pull up a baobab seedling too late, you can never get rid of it. It will take over the whole planet. Its roots can drill through the planet, and if the planet is small and there are many baobab trees, it will shatter the whole planet. "It's a matter of discipline," the Little Prince later explained to me. "When you've finished washing up in the morning, you must carefully wash up the planet, and you must make a rule to pull up the baobab seedlings on time. One day, he encouraged me to draw a beautiful picture so that the children in my hometown would have a deep impression of this. He also told me, “This will be very useful if they travel someday. So, based on the Little Prince’s description, I drew this planet. I’ve never been one to speak in a moralistic tone, but the danger of baobab trees is not widely understood, and it’s extremely dangerous for those lost on asteroids. Therefore, this time, I boldly broke my usual habit of not lecturing. I said, “Children, beware of those baobab trees!” To warn my friends of this danger—a danger they, like myself, have long encountered without realizing its severity—I put a lot of effort into drawing this picture. The lesson I’m presenting is very significant, and the effort was well worth it. You might ask, why aren’t the other drawings in this book as magnificent as this one? The answer was simple: I had tried to paint other pictures better, but without success. But when I painted the baobab tree, a sense of urgency motivated me.

VI. Ah! Little Prince, that's how I gradually came to understand your melancholy life. For a long time, your only pleasure was watching the gentle sunset. This new detail I learned on the morning of the fourth day. You said to me then:

“I love watching the sunset. Let's go watch a sunset!”

“But we have to wait…”

“Wait for what?”

“For the sun to go down.”

At first, you seemed very surprised, then you laughed at your own confusion. You said to me:

“I always thought I was in my hometown!”

Indeed, everyone knows that in America it's noon, and in France it's sunset; you can see the sunset if you get to France within a minute. Unfortunately, France is so far away. But on your little asteroid, you only need to move your chair a few steps. That way, you can see the sunset whenever you want…

Here are four shoes that are destroying your feet. I see folks wearing these every single day. Every single one of them tells me the same thing: the bump keeps growing, the pain keeps spreading, and nobody can tell me why.

Number one. Crocs. I know why you wear these. They are easy. They are comfortable. You slip them on and you do not think about it. That is exactly the problem. In Chinese medicine, we say the feet are the roots of the body. Your roots need to feel the earth. These are blocks of plastic foam that shut off the sensory feedback your feet need to balance. Your foot muscles get lazy, your ankles get weak, and you are destabilizing your entire body. And that wide open hole in the back? Your heel slides around with every step, forcing your toes to claw and grip the front to keep the shoe on. That bump? It is not growing because of genetics. It is growing because this shoe turned off the muscles that were keeping it straight.

Number two. New Balance Walking Shoes. The ones your doctor recommended. Look at the heel. Raised almost an inch. Every single step, that raised heel shifts all your body weight forward onto the balls of your feet and your toes. Your big toe is supposed to anchor your entire body. When all that weight is forced onto it, eight hours a day, the joint has no choice but to push outward. That is where your bump comes from. Your doctor meant well. But this shoe is feeding the problem every time you put it on.

Number three. Brooks Ghost or Adrenaline. Maximum cushioning, high heel drop, curved sole. That curve forces your foot to roll forward unnaturally. You are squeezing your big toe into a point for forty years and wondering why the joint is pushing outward. This shoe does not protect your feet. It deforms them slowly.

Number four. Hoka. Folks spend a hundred and eighty dollars specifically because their feet hurt. But the sole is over an inch thick. Your foot cannot feel anything. The muscles that hold your toes in alignment stop firing completely. And that narrow shape up front is still crushing your toes together. You are paying a hundred and eighty dollars to make the problem worse in comfort. That is the cruelest part.

Every one of these companies knows this. They sell cushioning because it feels good in the store. They do not care what it does to your feet over ten years.

title: See Why Parents Are Ditching Fluoride Toothpaste
body:
Your child has been brushing with fluoride since age three. Maybe earlier. They can't control their swallowing reflex until age six. Studies show kids ages 3-6 swallow 26-30% of their toothpaste every brush. Toddlers under two swallow nearly all of it. Their developing brains retain 80-90% of the fluoride they ingest. Adults only retain 50-60%.

The NTP reviewed decades of research and concluded that higher fluoride exposure is associated with lower IQ in children. Harvard reviewed 27 studies and found kids in high-fluoride areas scored 7 IQ points lower.
